defaults.permitted_development: Agricultural buildings in England can benefit from Part 6 permitted development rights where the land is a genuine agricultural unit and the proposal is reasonably necessary for agriculture, but many schemes still require prior approval on siting, design and external appearance. The practical farming case, siting and external appearance usually matter more than a single dimension on plan.

rules.height_rules: For many Part 6 schemes the overall height should not exceed 12m, with much tighter limits near safeguarded aerodromes. Ridge height, eaves height and roof pitch all need checking before assuming the right applies.
rules.depth_rules: There is no householder-style depth rule. What matters is whether the span, footprint and scale remain reasonably necessary for the agricultural unit rather than becoming an oversized industrial shed.
rules.boundary_rules: Agricultural buildings should not be sited so close to roads, homes or other sensitive neighbours that traffic, odour, noise or visual impact becomes unacceptable. Proximity to classified roads and protected buildings can limit or remove the Part 6 route. The practical farming case, siting and external appearance usually matter more than a single dimension on plan.
rules.roof_rules: Roof form is judged through overall height, bulk and any prior-approval considerations. Large reflective roofs or bulky ridges can be the point at which a farm building stops looking acceptable in the landscape.
rules.materials_rules: Use practical agricultural materials and muted colours that reduce glare and help the building sit quietly in the rural landscape rather than reading as commercial cladding. The practical farming case, siting and external appearance usually matter more than a single dimension on plan.

rules.permitted_development: In Broxbourne, Part 6 only goes so far: the building still needs to be reasonably necessary for the holding and not just a large general-purpose shed pushed close to housing or roads.

rules.height_rules: In Broxbourne, the legal maximum may be 12m for many Part 6 schemes, but prior approval usually turns on whether ridge and eaves height feel proportionate beside nearby housing and roads.
rules.depth_rules: There is no simple householder-style depth rule. What matters is whether the span, footprint and scale remain reasonably necessary for the unit rather than sliding into an oversized industrial shed.
rules.boundary_rules: In Broxbourne, separation from homes, access roads and the handling of traffic, lighting and service yards usually matter more at the boundary than the shed footprint alone.
rules.roof_rules: Roof form is assessed through overall height, bulk and prior-approval considerations. Large reflective roofs or bulky ridges can be the point at which an agricultural building stops looking acceptable in the landscape.
rules.materials_rules: Use practical agricultural materials and muted colours that reduce glare and help the building sit quietly in open countryside rather than reading as commercial cladding. The practical farming case, siting and external appearance usually matter more than a single dimension on plan.

restrictions.conservation_area: Agricultural development in or near a conservation area can face closer scrutiny on siting, scale, colour and landscape impact even where Part 6 rights may exist.
restrictions.listed_building: Works affecting a listed farm building, its curtilage or setting can need listed building consent and a separate planning assessment even where agricultural rights are otherwise available.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions can remove fallback rights for farm development in selected locations, so the site designation should be checked before relying on Part 6.
